title: Wonder Without Exaggeration
paragraphs: The octopus has become a favourite of popular science, and favourites are dangerous subjects, because affection encourages us to repeat striking claims without checking them. A careful reading of reliable sources separates the solid from the shaky. This article tries to follow that advice.

The solid facts concern the animal's anatomy. It has three hearts: two pump blood through the gills, and the third circulates it through the rest of the body. Its blood is blue because it carries oxygen on a copper-based protein, hemocyanin, where human blood relies on the iron-based hemoglobin. Hemocyanin appears to perform efficiently in cold, poorly oxygenated water, which suggests an adaptation rather than a curiosity. None of these facts needs embellishment to impress a thoughtful reader.

The shakier claims concern the nervous system. It is well established that a large share of an octopus's neurons sits in its arms; PBS puts the figure at about two thirds, while other sources offer lower proportions. The popular slogan that the animal has nine brains compresses this distribution into a vivid but misleading image, since a cluster of neurons in an arm is not a brain in any ordinary sense. A more accurate phrase would be that the animal has one central brain and a widely distributed nervous system.

Why do these distinctions matter? Because the gap between a measured fact and a memorable claim is where misunderstanding grows. An audience told that the octopus has nine brains may conclude that it thinks nine times as well, an inference the evidence does not support.

The fairest summary is therefore modest: the octopus organises its body and its nervous system very differently from vertebrates, and that difference is fascinating without needing exaggeration. Scientific wonder survives precision perfectly well; indeed, it usually deepens with it. Readers lose nothing by demanding that standard, and they gain a clearer picture of the animal.
